conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time to talk with me today. My name is Dr. Martinez, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I spend my days helping new mothers sort through the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives.

To get a clear picture of how you’ve been feeling lately, I’d like to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—you may hear it called the EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand what’s true for you so we can decide together what kind of support would feel most helpful.

Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. If at any point a question feels hard to answer, we can pause or rephrase it—whatever helps you feel most comfortable.

When you’re ready, we’ll move through the ten questions one by one. I’ll ask them conversationally, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly… I can laugh sometimes, but it’s like the joy gets cut in half. My sister sent me a silly video yesterday and I chuckled, but then it just fizzled out and I felt flat again. Most of the day nothing feels truly funny—more like I’m going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very much. I laughed a little once or twice, but even when something is funny, the laughter feels kind of distant, like I’m watching myself instead of really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more chore. I still try to plan one or two things so I don’t feel totally stuck, but the “looking-forward” part just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I instantly think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I ate the wrong food or didn’t read his cues fast enough. Even when my partner says it’s normal infant stuff, I keep replaying it in my head and telling myself I should be better at this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing—then I watch his chest and count breaths until I can talk myself down. Or I worry the stroller will roll into traffic, or that I’ll drop him, even when nothing’s happening. I know it’s probably irrational, but I can’t turn the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, several times. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen even though I can’t name what. Last night I was rocking the baby and out of nowhere I pictured him just slipping from my arms; my heart started pounding so hard I had to sit on the floor and breathe through my mouth until it passed.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Between the night-wakings, the endless laundry, and feeling like I have to keep it together for the baby, it piles up fast. I’ll start one task and get pulled into three others, then feel like I’m drowning. Sometimes I just stare at the mess and think, “I can’t do this,” but I still push through because I have to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—mostly worries about the baby or replaying everything I think I messed up that day. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and when I do I wake up at least once or twice with my heart racing from anxious dreams. By morning I feel like I’ve barely rested even if the baby slept a decent stretch.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s how I feel most of the day—like there’s a heavy blanket on me. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but right behind it is this sadness I can’t shake. It’s not always crying-level awful, just a constant “down” that makes everything feel gray.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I put him in the crib for a nap, sat on the couch, and just burst into tears for no clear reason. The other time was after a phone call with my mom—she asked how I was doing and I said “fine,” but as soon as I hung up I started sobbing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

...A couple of times, yeah. Nothing I planned or anything like that—just these quick flashes, like "what if I just kept driving past the house and never came back," or "what if I just didn't wake up." They scare me when they pop in, and I push them away, but they have shown up.

Hearing how hard these early weeks have been for you-how the laughter feels distant, how even simple joys seem heavy-tells me you're carrying far more than anyone should alone. Your honesty about the racing worries, the sudden tears, and those scary thoughts of escape shows remarkable strength, and it's clear you want to feel better for both yourself and your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports marked reduction in ability to laugh and feel genuine amusement, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment; "Hardly at all" best captures her statement that "the looking-forward part just isn't there."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, pervasive self-blame across multiple situations, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, irrational worries that she cannot control, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes occurring "several times" with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent struggle ('most days') and feeling overwhelmed, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to distressing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the day" and a constant "down" mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying twice in the past week due to unhappiness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day (<quote>heavy blanket</quote>), markedly diminished interest (<quote>looking-forward part just isn't there</quote>), guilt, recurrent thoughts of death, sleep disturbance, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating. Co-occurring <med>anxiety symptoms</med> and panic attacks are also present. Item 10 score of 1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Request urgent perinatal mental-health referral for therapy and medication review if indicated
3. Develop a written safety plan with your clinician; keep crisis hotline numbers in your phone
4. Share your responses with a trusted partner or family member so they can help monitor mood
5. Prioritise 4-hour uninterrupted rest once daily; consider split-night partner shifts
6. Practice brief grounding exercises when panic rises (slow breathing, naming five objects you can see)
7. Continue attending mother-baby groups or peer support; isolation worsens symptoms
8. Schedule a two-week follow-up EPDS to track progress after interventions start
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Summary – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Demographic: Postpartum mother (infant <12 mo)

Screening Tool: EPDS-10 (patient narrative responses)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked loss of enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Intrusive, irrational worries; panic attacks; nocturnal hyper-arousal  
- Sleep initiation/maintenance disturbance (mood-related)  
- Frequent “overwhelm,” difficulty coping with routine tasks  
- Passive self-harm ideation without intent or plan

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms, postpartum onset.

Screening significance  
- Meets DSM-5-TR criteria threshold for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset (screening level)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms/panic attacks  
- Safety concern: presence of self-harm cognitions, denied intent/plan

Risk factors noted  
- Sleep deprivation secondary to mood  
- Lack of perceived support (brief mention)  
- First-person maternal expectations of competence

Safety  
Passive suicidal ideation reported; requires immediate risk assessment and safety planning.

Recommendation  
Refer for urgent psychiatric evaluation and follow-up care; consider EPDS scoring for severity tracking; provide crisis resources and support contacts.

Clinician: [Name, Credentials]
